extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, constitutional theory, and history of political thought
extracted.subtask_description: Critical evaluation of Montesquieu's Esprit des lois and its political and social doctrines, focusing on principles such as separation of powers, forms of government, penal reform, slavery, tolerance, and the state's duty to the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers as condition of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Les trois pouvoirs sont-ils réunis, c'est le despotisme; séparés, c'est la liberté." The constitution of England is founded on the separation of powers and is therefore a free constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation of executive, legislative and judicial powers is presented as the fundamental principle of a free government. The author defends the principle while acknowledging practical complications and multiple possible divisions and combinations depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Si la puissance de juger était jointe à la législative, le pouvoir sur la vie et la liberté des citoyens serait arbitraire... si elle était jointe à la puissance exécutrice, le juge pourrait avoir la force d'un oppresseur."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judiciary must be absolutely independent from sovereign power to prevent arbitrariness and oppression; this is presented as a primary and indisputable principle of moderate government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of executive and legislative powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the one who has force makes the laws, he can make them tyrannical; similarly if the legislature holds force, it can become oppressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executive should not make laws directly; even if executive power emanates from the people, it should not be exercised directly by them. Separation is necessary to prevent tyranny whether power is in a monarch or in the people/assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish separation of powers from mixed government
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse the theory of separation of powers with the theory of mixed (threefold) governments: the former concerns functions (executive, legislative, judicial), the latter concerns social bodies (king, nobility, people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify terms: Montesquieu blends two distinct theories (powers vs. social estates); accurate analysis must keep these senses distinct when evaluating constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual checks and necessary overlap for action
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough to separate powers; they must be united and accorded. Independence requires that each have some share in the action of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A purely isolated separation leads to impotence; if the legislature can do nothing on the executive the latter becomes vain, and vice versa. Practical constitutions should give each branch limited influence over others to ensure both liberty and effective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable friction/slowdown as a safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Resistance and a slowing of affairs are not faults but virtues: 'Le ralentissement dans les affaires humaines, ce n'est pas un mal, c'est un bien.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation, reflection and reciprocal resistance increase chances for truth and reduce error. Institutional frictions that produce delay are valuable checks on rash action and concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of separation—cannot prevent all abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation of powers prevents certain abuses but not all; if the three powers collude, separation alone offers no guarantee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that constitutional machinery cannot render impossible every abuse; other safeguards (representation of broad interests, public opinion/press) and moral forces are needed to restrain collusion among branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion/press as ultimate guarantor
rubrics_metrics.description: When constitutional guarantees fail, 'l'opinion exprimée par la presse' is the last guarantee of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External moral and social forces—public opinion, free press—act as a corrective when formal separations are insufficient, limiting the scope of oppression to narrower interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should be tempered (moderation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'government tempéré' combining elements of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy is desirable; moderation is the principle of separation of powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While endorsing a tempered constitution, the critic questions Montesquieu's literal insistence on particular institutional elements (hereditary monarchy, true nobility) as necessary conditions for liberty; plurality of combinations is possible and depends on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty does not require social privilege (aristocracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioning Montesquieu's implication that aristocracy (privilege) is a political principle necessary for freedom: 'La liberté politique ne peut-elle s'acheter que par l'inégalité sociale?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that increasing civil equality should not be seen as inimical to liberty; aristocracy as privilege may not be necessary, and merit/experience-based leadership may simply be democracy, not true aristocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softening of criminal penalties and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Severity of penalties suits despotism; in moderate governments shame and prevention should be stronger than extreme punishments. 'Dans les bons gouvernements, il vaut mieux prévenir que punir.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cruel and disproportionate punishments corrupt the state and blunt moral sensibilities; penal law should be humane, proportionate, oriented to prevention and consistent with liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of torture
rubrics_metrics.description: Torture is not necessary: Montesquieu treats torture briefly but points out that a civilized nation can reject it: 'Nous voyons aujourd'hui, une nation très bien policée la rejeter sans inconvénient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if Montesquieu frames torture as fitting despotism, the implication is a moral denunciation of torture and a call for its abolition in civilized states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of slavery and its illegitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery cannot be justified by right of war, contract, or birth; 'La loi de l'esclavage est toujours contre l'esclave, jamais pour lui.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu's arguments: the vanquished are not necessarily subject to death; sale presupposes price and benefit which do not exist for slaves; slavery violates natural equality and public freedom. The critic credits Montesquieu with pioneering forceful anti-slavery argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious toleration
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tolérer une religion, ce n'est pas l'approuver.' In a state requiring unity and peace, different religions must be tolerated, i.e., live in peace without proscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious persecution and forced conversion tear the state apart; toleration is a political prudence and a moral imperative to prevent civil strife and protect conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: State obligation to assure subsistence through work
rubrics_metrics.description: The State must ensure citizens' subsistence not by mere alms but by providing work or teaching them to work: 'Un État bien policé tire cette subsistance du fond des arts mêmes: il donne aux uns les travaux dont ils sont capables, il enseigne aux autres à travailler.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu balances against both extreme charity and laissez-faire: the state should favor employment and vocational education to secure subsistence; excessive hospitals/alms may foster idleness. The critic notes this anticipates later economic thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political principles cannot substitute for civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: No political machine can remedy every abuse; government survives by the goodwill and love of those who support it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions require citizens' attachment to country and public spirit; absence of civic virtue can cause degeneration into conflict and civil war, beyond what constitutional design alone can prevent.
